Lessons.Title: Standard Deviation
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: understand population standard deviation as a measure of spread, calculate it for small sets and verify a technology result; distinguish it from MAD and the sample standard deviation. Independently authored Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 1 Lesson 12, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/1/12/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). Source roles: Building On HSS-ID.A.1 and HSS-ID.A.2; Addressing HSS-ID.A.2 and HSS-ID.A.3.

Use the population standard deviation convention in this unit: for n observations, calculate mean μ, find each (x−μ)², average those squared distances by dividing by n, and take the square root. This gives σ, in the original units. Dividing by n−1 is the alternative sample-standard-deviation calculation and must not be silently substituted.

Original hypothetical datasets: A=3,3,5,5 and B=1,1,7,7. Both have mean 4. In A, squared deviations are 1,1,1,1 so population variance is 1 and σ=1. In B the squared deviations are 9,9,9,9 so variance is 9 and σ=3. B is more variable even though mean is identical.

Student task: construct original dot plots, compare standard deviation with MAD, then use statistical software with the population-SD option to verify A and B. Explore replacing B by four copies of the constant 4 and explain why σ becomes zero. Use a teacher-scored explanation for what the units and comparative magnitude mean.

Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 for correct mean, squared-deviation table and division by n, correct square root with units, meaningful A/B comparison and honest software-check evidence (max 8). A single numeric result does not prove software use or contextual understanding.

Source-activity A/B review, IM Algebra 1 First Edition U01:L12: Describe three data displays; explain technology-derived standard deviation and compare with MAD; distinguish population from sample convention. Keep original first-party mathematical material and graphics; source artwork identity is NOT claimed. All physical/technology/partner work remains NOT_PERFORMED unless observed.

KeyConcepts.Title: Population standard deviation
KeyConcepts.Definition: The square root of the average squared distance from the population mean.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use n in the denominator for the population definition used here.

KeyConcepts.Title: Population versus sample SD
KeyConcepts.Definition: Population σ uses division by n, whereas sample s typically uses n−1.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check which statistic a software function reports.
KeyConcepts.Example: For 3,3,5,5, population SD=1, while sample SD is sqrt(4/3).

KeyConcepts.Title: Zero variation
KeyConcepts.Definition: If every observation equals the same constant, variance and SD are zero.

WorkedExamples.Title: Calculate population SD for A
WorkedExamples.Question: Find σ for 3,3,5,5.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the given original data, show the computation and interpret the result in context.
Steps: Divide by n=4 to obtain variance 1.
Square root gives σ=1 in the original unit.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare SD for B
WorkedExamples.Question: Find σ for 1,1,7,7 and compare it with A.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the given original data, show the computation and interpret the result in context.
WorkedExamples.Answer: B SD=3; it is three times A's population SD.
WorkedExamples.Check: Squared deviations and the square root are verified.

WorkedExamples.Title: Recognize zero spread
WorkedExamples.Question: Compute σ for four copies of 4.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the given original data, show the computation and interpret the result in context.
Steps: All four deviations from mean are zero.
WorkedExamples.Check: All values are identical, which is exactly the zero-variability condition.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Dividing by n−1 in a population-SD exercise
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the source's n convention; label sample s if using n−1.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Average squared deviations is variance in squared units, not SD.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Take the nonnegative square root to return to original units.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming same mean implies same variability
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Distribution means say nothing about how far values lie from center.

SummaryPoints: Population SD uses n in the denominator and returns to original units after a square root.
Both original datasets have mean 4 but SDs 1 and 3.
A constant dataset has SD zero; greater positive SD indicates greater spread.
Technology can verify a calculation but teacher review is needed for explanation.
